prize_parts.citation: for establishing that biomolecular condensates form by liquid-liquid phase separation, a physical-chemical principle for organizing the interior of cells
for the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: My opening first choice, B044, remains the one I can defend most strongly on conceptual grounds. Brangwynne and Hyman showed that P granules and nucleoli behave as liquids, and that observation recast intracellular organisation as a phase-behaviour problem governed by multivalency, interfacial tension and concentration thresholds. Few discoveries in the last twenty years have changed how biochemists, cell biologists and soft-matter physicists frame the same question. I now pair it with B058 because, reading the openings, ionizable lipid nanoparticles are the candidate with the broadest support across the table (four members placed it in their top three, and it is the highest Borda total on the shortlist), and its scientific core is lipid self-assembly: pKa-tuned lipids that are neutral in circulation, charged in the endosome, and drive non-lamellar phase transitions and membrane fusion for release. A two-part prize pairing a new concept of organisation inside the cell with a molecular-design principle for crossing the membrane is a balanced Chemistry prize that sits in physical and biological chemistry rather than synthesis alone.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation about B044 is that the field is still sorting out what is genuinely equilibrium phase separation in vivo versus other assemblies, and that the three-person limit forces us to leave out Rosen, Pappu and Mittag, whose multivalency and sequence-grammar work gives the concept its quantitative backbone. For B058 the strongest objection is attribution: the Vancouver lineage (Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan) and the MIT lineage (Anderson, Langer) overlap with patents and industry, and the 2023 Medicine prize on mRNA modification may lead colleagues to read delivery as already honoured. Naming only Cullis is clean on paper but arguably unfair to Hope and Madden, and a two-part split of three places is a strained compromise on both sides.

responses.point: Heiner ranks halide perovskites first for a clear underlying principle, a quantitative route to practical limits and a large generative potential, while placing biomolecular phase separation seventh.
responses.response: I agree the perovskite story has a real principle behind it and rapid, reproduced progress, and I kept it as an alternative. My hesitation is the one he himself flags: the priority order among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grazel and Seok is a genuine dispute, and operational stability and lead toxicity are unresolved, so I cannot see a clean three-person prize today. On phase separation I would push back on ranking it seventh. Its quantitative content is substantial (binodals, critical concentrations, valency-dependent thresholds) and it generates predictions in biology in the same way he values for perovskites. I would like to hear which part he finds less mature.

responses.point: Peter ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N cross-coupling first as a general, ligand-controlled method used throughout medicinal and process chemistry, distinct from the 2010 cross-coupling prize, with Kosugi recognised in the citation rather than as a laureate.
responses.response: I share his view that the method is mature and widely used, and that Buchwald and Hartwig are the clear independent originators; I ranked it fifth for that reason. Where I differ is on how much the 2010 prize counts. Although the C-N reaction is a distinct advance, a second cross-coupling award within sixteen years sits awkwardly beside the argument that the prize should also represent physical and biological chemistry, which have fewer recent awards than synthesis. I also note his Kosugi handling is a priority judgement, since the stoichiometric tin-amide chemistry came first. I would support it as a strong alternative if our appetite is for a synthesis prize, but I would not put it ahead of a concept-level discovery.

responses.point: Andrei ranks massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis first because its enabling steps (reversible terminators, modified dNTPs, cluster readout) are concrete nucleotide chemistry with transformative biological reach, while also ranking ionizable lipid nanoparticles second.
responses.response: I agree with him on lipid nanoparticles and I am glad that we converge there, since it is the strongest area of overlap on the table. On sequencing I accept the chemistry, but I ranked it last on my list because the impact is realised through instruments and platforms across competing lineages (Solexa, 454, Ju, Mayer), and any three-person cut leaves out serious claimants. I would ask him whether anchoring on Balasubramanian and Klenerman alone is defensible given that his own opening adds Rothberg, because that choice is where this candidate is decided.

responses.point: Johan ranks base editing first as a new chemical approach to genome editing, deamination by an engineered enzyme fused to a Cas nickase, with Liu as the intellectual driver and Komor and Gaudelli as lead trainees.
responses.response: I take the chemical point seriously, and the elegance of the nucleobase deamination is real. My concern is timing and framing: it follows the 2020 CRISPR prize closely, and clinical outcomes are still preliminary. Whether Komor and Gaudelli should receive credit as trainees rather than Kondo and Nishida's independent work is also unresolved. I would rather wait for the clinical record than risk reading as an incremental refinement of a recent award, though I accept that this is a judgement about maturity and not about the quality of the science.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a single coherent achievement to a two-part prize that is partly a compromise between my first choice and the candidate with the widest support.
How far the Cullis group's claim on ionizable-lipid design can be separated from Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and whether naming one person is defensible.
Whether the in-vivo evidence for liquid-like condensates is strong enough to cite the principle without qualification, and whether Rosen should replace Brangwynne or Hyman in a one-part prize.
How much weight the 2023 Medicine prize and 2020 and 2024 Chemistry prizes should carry against delivery lipids, base editing and protein folding.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I note that my research on lipid self-assembly and lipid-protein co-assembly is close in subject to B058 and B044, and that I share Lund with two other members; I have no known personal or institutional tie to any of the credited people.
